subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Drying Phase
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Drying Phase.

hook.text: The first phase of roasting is just drying. Green beans start at 8–12% moisture that must evaporate before browning begins.

buildup.text: For the first 4–5 minutes, the bean absorbs heat but shows little visible change. It's storing energy.

discovery.text: The bean slowly turns from green to yellow as chlorophyll breaks down and water escapes as steam.

twist.text: Rushing the drying phase creates 'baked' coffee—flat, papery flavor. Patience here sets up the entire roast.

climax.text: Only after sufficient drying can the Maillard reaction and caramelization begin. Drying is the invisible foundation.

punchline.text: Nothing visible is happening yet. Everything is being prepared. Drying is essential.

quiz.question: What happens if the drying phase is rushed?
options: Flat, papery 'baked' coffee with muted flavor

details.summary: The drying phase is the first stage of roasting, during which moisture inside the green bean evaporates. Beans turn from green to yellow and begin to smell like toasted bread. Proper drying sets the foundation for even development later.
details.whyItMatters: Rushing or uneven drying leads to baked or scorched beans later in the roast. Mastering this quiet phase is essential for consistent, flavorful results.
takeaways: Beans lose most of their moisture during the drying phase
Color shifts from green to yellow as water evaporates
Even drying prevents defects in later roast stages

faq.question: How long does the drying phase typically last during roasting?
faq.answer: The drying phase usually lasts four to eight minutes depending on batch size, drum temperature, and the moisture content of the green beans. It ends when the beans turn uniformly yellow.

faq.question: What happens if the drying phase is too short or too long?
faq.answer: Too short a drying phase traps moisture inside the bean, causing uneven development and grassy flavors. Too long a phase bakes the bean, resulting in flat, dull flavors with muted acidity.
